newsitem.title: GUAM: Grieving KAL victim families reach Guam.
newsitem.headline: Grieving KAL victim families reach Guam.

text.p: Hysterical mourners mixed with holidaymakers on Thursday as hundreds of Koreans arrived in Guam to claim the bodies of loved ones lost in the fiery crash of Korean Airlines Flight 801.

The 250 South Koreans who reached the island 24 hours after friends and family went down in the jungle included wailing old women in black mourning garb, stone-faced KAL officials and a group of Seoul nurses flown in to help.
Dressed in dark, heavy suits despite stultifying heat, a small group of Korean parliamentarians came to mourn a colleague, lawmaker Shi Ki-ha, among the more than 200 who died in the jungle blaze.
Assemblywomen, like most of their male compatriots, put on stoic faces -- in contrast to the Korean women, many of whom sobbed or even screamed.
"What will I do now? How will I live on?" shrieked an elderly Korean woman, who nearly collapsed in the airport arrival lounge.
In an odd juxtaposition of tourism and tragedy, giggling young Japanese package tourists mingled with the bereaved at the airport exit, seemingly oblivious to the funeral atmosphere.
Nearby, airport police scrambled to surround a Korean man whose shouts punctuated the airport and who looked about to punch out a hapless KAL employee.

"Many suspect the airline wants to shunt them off to a quiet room, give them a quick explanation and pack them back off to Seoul," explained Sandra Kim, a Korean resident of Guam. "We think they deserve the full story."

Kim, a volunteer translator, said most of the relatives from Korea wanted to go either to the crash site, a makeshift memorial altar in the Guam capital, or to the two hospitals where 27 survivors of the fiery crash were being treated.
At a tense news conference on Wednesday, KAL vice-president Shim In-taek was all but shouted down by Korean relatives as he apologised and briefed them on the crash.
The airline had set up a hospitality and information centre for the bereaved and promised regular briefings. But many family members of victims demanded more and better information.
"The airline seems to be passing the buck at a time when families need them the most," said Roger Kang, a vacationing Seoul businessman who was helping families of victims.
"Many of them still have not seen a proper list of who has survived and who is dead."
James Lee, an official of the 10,000-member Guam Korean Residents Association, said that, the anguish of the moment aside, Koreans tend to mistrust KAL "for its past record of accidents".
Kang, however, shrugged off any suggestion Wednesday's crash affirmed outsiders' perceptions that his country's national carrier had a poor safety record.
"What happened is what happened, but its the lack of responsibility afterward that angers us."
